title: Subject-matter and objectives
content: This Regulation lays down rules relating to the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and rules relating to the free movement of personal data.
key_obligations: Protect the fundamental rights of natural persons
Ensure the free movement of data within the EU
sanctions: No specific sanction - general scope article
practical_examples: A French e-commerce site must comply with GDPR for all processing of its European customers' data

title: Material scope
content: This Regulation applies to the processing of personal data wholly or partly by automated means and to the processing other than by automated means of personal data which form part of a filing system.
key_obligations: Identify all automated and non-automated processing
Verify whether the processing falls within the scope of the GDPR
sanctions: Non-application of the GDPR for processing outside scope
practical_examples: An Excel file containing customer names is subject to the GDPR

title: Territorial scope
content: This Regulation applies to the processing of personal data in the context of the activities of an establishment of a controller or processor in the Union, regardless of whether the processing takes place in the Union or not.
key_obligations: Extraterritorial application of the GDPR
Designate a representative in the EU if necessary
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: A US company selling online to French customers must comply with the GDPR

title: Definitions
content: For the purposes of this Regulation: personal data, processing, restriction of processing, profiling, pseudonymisation, filing system, controller, processor, recipient, third party, consent, personal data breach, genetic data, biometric data, data concerning health, etc.
key_obligations: Master the 26 key definitions of the GDPR
Distinguish between controller and processor
sanctions: No direct sanction but fundamental for interpretation
practical_examples: An IP address is personal data under the GDPR
A cookie identifying a user constitutes personal data

title: Principles relating to processing of personal data
content: Personal data shall be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently; collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes; adequate, relevant and limited; accurate and kept up to date; kept for no longer than necessary; processed ensuring appropriate security.
key_obligations: Lawfulness, fairness, transparency
Purpose limitation
Data minimisation
Accuracy
Storage limitation
Integrity and confidentiality
Accountability
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover (Article 83(5))
practical_examples: Only collect data strictly necessary for a registration form

title: Lawfulness of processing
content: Processing shall be lawful only if at least one condition applies: consent, performance of a contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public interest, legitimate interests.
key_obligations: Identify a legal basis for each processing operation
Document the chosen legal basis
Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Consent for newsletters
Contract performance for delivery
Legal obligation for invoicing

title: Conditions for consent
content: The controller shall be able to demonstrate that the data subject has consented. The request for consent shall be presented clearly distinguishable, in an intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language.
key_obligations: Be able to demonstrate consent
Present the request clearly
Allow withdrawal at any time
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Cookie banner with granular choices
Unticked checkbox for newsletter subscription

title: Conditions applicable to child's consent
content: In relation to the offer of information society services directly to a child, processing shall be lawful where the child is at least 16 years old. Below that age, parental consent is required.
key_obligations: Verify the age of minor users
Obtain parental consent for under-16s (varies by member state)
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: A social network must verify age during registration
TikTok was fined for processing children's data

title: Processing of special categories of personal data
content: Processing of data revealing racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, genetic data, biometric data, health data, sex life or sexual orientation is prohibited, except for limited exceptions.
key_obligations: Prohibition in principle of processing sensitive data
Identify applicable exceptions
Enhanced security measures
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: A hospital processing health data must justify an exception
An employer cannot collect employees' political opinions

title: Processing of data relating to criminal convictions
content: Processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences may only be carried out under the control of official authority or when authorised by Union or Member State law.
key_obligations: Processing under control of official authority
Authorisation by national or EU law required
sanctions: Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: An employer can only request a criminal record check if the law permits it

title: Processing which does not require identification
content: If the purposes for which a controller processes personal data do not require identification of a data subject, the controller is not obliged to maintain additional information to identify the data subject.
key_obligations: No obligation to maintain identification data if unnecessary
sanctions: No specific sanction
practical_examples: Anonymised statistics not requiring re-identification

chapter: Chapter III - Rights of the Data Subject
title: Transparent information, communication and modalities
content: The controller shall take appropriate measures to provide information and any communication in a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language.
key_obligations: Provide information concisely and transparently
Respond within one month
Free of charge exercise of rights
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Privacy policy in clear and accessible language

chapter: Chapter III - Rights of the Data Subject
title: Information to be provided where data are collected from the data subject
content: When collecting data from the data subject, the controller shall provide: identity of the controller, purposes, legal basis, recipients, transfers outside the EU, retention period, rights.
key_obligations: Inform at the time of collection
Specify the identity of the controller and DPO
State the purposes and legal basis
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Information notices under contact forms
Privacy policy accessible from every page

chapter: Chapter III - Rights of the Data Subject
title: Information where data have not been obtained from the data subject
content: Where data have not been obtained from the data subject, the controller shall provide the information within a reasonable period (maximum one month), including the source of the data.
key_obligations: Inform within a reasonable period
Indicate the source of the data
Specify the categories of data processed
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Informing a prospect whose data came from a commercial partner

chapter: Chapter III - Rights of the Data Subject
title: Right of access by the data subject
content: The data subject has the right to obtain confirmation as to whether personal data are being processed and access to the data together with information about the processing.
key_obligations: Confirm or deny the processing of data
Provide a copy of the data
Respond within one month
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: A customer requests a list of all data the company holds about them

chapter: Chapter III - Rights of the Data Subject
title: Right to rectification
content: The data subject has the right to obtain rectification of inaccurate personal data and to have incomplete personal data completed.
key_obligations: Rectify inaccurate data without delay
Complete incomplete data
Inform recipients of rectifications
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Correcting an incorrect email address in a customer file

chapter: Chapter III - Rights of the Data Subject
title: Right to erasure (right to be forgotten)
content: The data subject has the right to obtain erasure of personal data where data are no longer necessary, consent is withdrawn, the data subject objects, processing is unlawful, or a legal obligation requires it.
key_obligations: Erase data without undue delay
Inform other controllers of the erasure request
Exceptions: freedom of expression, legal obligation, public interest
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Deletion of a user account and all associated data
Right to be forgotten on a search engine

chapter: Chapter III - Rights of the Data Subject
title: Right to restriction of processing
content: The data subject may obtain restriction of processing when accuracy is contested, processing is unlawful, the controller no longer needs the data, or the data subject has objected.
key_obligations: Restrict processing in the specified cases
Inform the data subject before lifting restriction
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Freezing customer data while accuracy is being verified

chapter: Chapter III - Rights of the Data Subject
title: Notification obligation regarding rectification or erasure
content: The controller shall communicate any rectification, erasure or restriction to each recipient unless this proves impossible or involves disproportionate effort.
key_obligations: Notify recipients of rectifications, erasures or restrictions
Inform the data subject of recipients if requested
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Informing a commercial partner of rectification of shared customer data

chapter: Chapter III - Rights of the Data Subject
title: Right to data portability
content: Data subjects have the right to receive their personal data in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format and to transmit it to another controller.
key_obligations: Provide data in a structured machine-readable format
Allow direct transmission to another controller
Applies to automated processing based on consent or contract
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Transferring data from one social network to another

chapter: Chapter III - Rights of the Data Subject
title: Right to object
content: The data subject may object at any time to processing based on public interest or legitimate interest. For direct marketing, the right to object is absolute.
key_obligations: Respect the right to object without delay
Absolute right of objection for direct marketing
Inform the data subject of this right
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Mandatory unsubscribe link in marketing emails

chapter: Chapter III - Rights of the Data Subject
title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
content: The data subject has the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them.
key_obligations: Do not make solely automated decisions with significant effects
Provide safeguards (human intervention, right to express point of view)
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Automated credit scoring requires human intervention
Automated CV screening must allow appeals

title: Responsibility of the controller
content: The controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure and demonstrate that processing is carried out in accordance with this Regulation.
key_obligations: Implement appropriate technical and organisational measures
Demonstrate compliance (accountability)
Review and update measures regularly
sanctions: Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Documented data protection policy
Regular security audits

title: Data protection by design and by default
content: The controller shall implement appropriate measures such as pseudonymisation to integrate data protection principles by design and apply the most protective settings by default.
key_obligations: Privacy by design: integrate protection from the outset
Privacy by default: most protective settings by default
Data minimisation by default
sanctions: Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Pseudonymisation of data in development environments
Maximum privacy settings by default

title: Joint controllers
content: Where two or more controllers jointly determine the purposes and means of processing, they are joint controllers and shall define their respective responsibilities by arrangement.
key_obligations: Define roles and responsibilities by agreement
Make the arrangement available to data subjects
sanctions: Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Two companies jointly organising an event and collecting data
Facebook and page administrators (CJEU Wirtschaftsakademie)

title: Representatives of controllers not established in the Union
content: Where Article 3(2) applies, the controller or processor shall designate in writing a representative in the Union.
key_obligations: Designate a representative in the EU
The representative is the point of contact for authorities and data subjects
sanctions: Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: A Chinese company selling in Europe must designate an EU representative

title: Processor
content: The controller shall use only processors providing sufficient guarantees. Processing by a processor shall be governed by a contract.
key_obligations: Choose a processor with sufficient guarantees
Formalise with written contract
Processor acts only on instructions
Prior authorisation for sub-processors
sanctions: Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Sub-processing contract with a cloud host (AWS, OVH)
Auditing sub-processors

title: Processing under the authority of the controller
content: Any person acting under the authority of the controller or processor who has access to personal data shall not process them except on instructions from the controller.
key_obligations: Processing only on instructions from the controller
Train personnel with access to data
sanctions: Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: An employee may only access customer data within the scope of their duties

title: Records of processing activities
content: Each controller shall maintain a record of processing activities containing: name of the controller, purposes, categories of data subjects and data, recipients, transfers, retention periods, security measures.
key_obligations: Maintain written records of processing
Make records available to the supervisory authority
Mandatory for organisations with more than 250 employees or high-risk processing
sanctions: Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Excel register or dedicated software listing all processing activities

title: Cooperation with the supervisory authority
content: The controller, processor and their representative shall cooperate with the supervisory authority at its request.
key_obligations: Cooperate with the supervisory authority on request
Provide information as requested
sanctions: Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Responding to questionnaires from the supervisory authority within deadlines

title: Security of processing
content: The controller and processor shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including pseudonymisation, encryption, confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience.
key_obligations: Pseudonymisation and encryption
Confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience
Rapid restoration capability
Regular testing
sanctions: Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: AES-256 encryption of databases
Business continuity plan
Annual penetration testing

title: Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority
content: In the case of a personal data breach, the controller shall notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.
key_obligations: Notification within 72 hours
Documentation of every breach
Description of the nature and measures taken
sanctions: Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Notification to the authority following a ransomware attack
Reporting a customer data leak

title: Communication of a personal data breach to the data subject
content: When a breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms, the controller shall communicate the breach to the data subject without undue delay.
key_obligations: Communication to data subjects in case of high risk
Clear description of the breach
Recommendations to mitigate effects
sanctions: Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Email to customers informing of a password leak

title: Data protection impact assessment (DPIA)
content: Where processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms, the controller shall carry out an assessment of the impact of the envisaged processing operations before the processing.
key_obligations: Carry out a DPIA before high-risk processing
Mandatory for: systematic evaluation, large-scale sensitive data, systematic monitoring
Consult the DPO
sanctions: Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: DPIA for a CCTV system
DPIA for large-scale health data processing

title: Prior consultation
content: The controller shall consult the supervisory authority when a DPIA indicates that the processing would result in a high risk if no measures were taken.
key_obligations: Consult the authority if residual risk remains high after DPIA
The authority has 8 weeks to respond
sanctions: Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Consulting the authority before deploying facial recognition

title: Designation of the data protection officer
content: The controller and processor shall designate a DPO where: processing is carried out by a public authority; core activities consist of large-scale regular and systematic monitoring; or core activities consist of large-scale processing of special categories of data.
key_obligations: Designate a DPO in mandatory cases
DPO may be internal or external
Publish and communicate DPO contact details
sanctions: Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Mandatory DPO for a government ministry
Mandatory for a hospital

title: Position of the data protection officer
content: The DPO shall be involved in all issues relating to data protection. The DPO shall not receive any instructions and shall not be dismissed or penalised for performing their tasks.
key_obligations: Involve the DPO in all data protection issues
Guarantee the DPO's independence
Provide necessary resources
sanctions: Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: The DPO is consulted before any new project involving personal data

title: Tasks of the data protection officer
content: DPO tasks: inform and advise, monitor compliance with the GDPR, advise on DPIAs, cooperate with the supervisory authority, act as the point of contact.
key_obligations: Inform and advise on GDPR obligations
Monitor compliance internally
Advise on DPIAs
Cooperate with the authority
sanctions: Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: The DPO conducts internal compliance audits
The DPO trains employees

title: Codes of conduct
content: Member States and supervisory authorities encourage the drawing up of codes of conduct intended to contribute to the proper application of the GDPR.
key_obligations: Encourage sectoral codes of conduct
Submit for approval to the authority
sanctions: No direct sanction
practical_examples: EU Cloud Code of Conduct

title: Certification
content: Member States and authorities encourage the establishment of data protection certification mechanisms, seals and marks. Certification is voluntary and valid for a maximum of 3 years.
key_obligations: Encourage certification mechanisms
Voluntary and accessible certification
Maximum validity of 3 years
sanctions: No direct sanction
practical_examples: ISO 27701 certification for privacy management

chapter: Chapter V - Transfers to Third Countries
title: General principle for transfers
content: A transfer to a third country may take place only if the conditions in this Chapter are complied with.
key_obligations: Ensure an adequate level of protection for transfers outside the EU
Use an appropriate transfer mechanism
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Using Standard Contractual Clauses for transfers to the US

chapter: Chapter V - Transfers to Third Countries
title: Transfers on the basis of an adequacy decision
content: A transfer may take place where the Commission has decided that the third country ensures an adequate level of protection.
key_obligations: Verify the existence of an adequacy decision
EU-US Data Privacy Framework since July 2023
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Transfers to the UK covered by an adequacy decision
Transfers to the US under the EU-US DPF

chapter: Chapter V - Transfers to Third Countries
title: Transfers subject to appropriate safeguards
content: In the absence of an adequacy decision, transfers are possible with appropriate safeguards: Standard Contractual Clauses, BCRs, approved codes of conduct or certifications.
key_obligations: Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs)
Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs)
Transfer Impact Assessment (TIA)
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: SCCs with a processor in India
BCRs for intra-group transfers

chapter: Chapter V - Transfers to Third Countries
title: Derogations for specific situations
content: Without an adequacy decision or safeguards, transfers may take place based on: explicit consent, contractual necessity, public interest, legal claims, vital interests, or public register.
key_obligations: Derogations to be interpreted strictly
Occasional and non-systematic use only
sanctions: Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover
practical_examples: Occasional data transfer for an employee's business trip

title: Supervisory authority
content: Each Member State shall provide for one or more independent public authorities responsible for monitoring the application of this Regulation.
key_obligations: Each Member State designates an independent authority
The authority must have sufficient resources
sanctions: No direct sanction - Member State obligation
practical_examples: The ICO is the UK authority
The BfDI is the German federal authority

title: Powers of supervisory authorities
content: Each supervisory authority has investigative powers, corrective powers, and authorisation and advisory powers.
key_obligations: Investigative and audit powers
Power to order provision of information
Power to impose fines
Power to suspend data flows to a third country
sanctions: The authority may impose sanctions under Articles 83 and 84
practical_examples: On-site inspections
Enforcement orders with compliance deadlines

title: Cooperation between the lead supervisory authority and other authorities
content: The lead supervisory authority shall cooperate with the other supervisory authorities concerned, endeavouring to reach consensus.
key_obligations: One-stop shop mechanism for cross-border processing
Lead authority is that of the main establishment
sanctions: No direct sanction - inter-authority procedure
practical_examples: The Irish DPC is the lead authority for Meta, Google, Apple

title: Consistency mechanism
content: Supervisory authorities cooperate among themselves and with the Commission through the consistency mechanism for the uniform application of the GDPR.
key_obligations: Consistent application of the GDPR
EDPB opinions in certain cases
Binding EDPB decisions in case of disagreement
sanctions: No direct sanction - procedural mechanism
practical_examples: The EDPB issues guidelines
Binding EDPB decision in the Meta/WhatsApp case

chapter: Chapter VIII - Remedies, Liability and Penalties
title: Right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority
content: Every data subject has the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority if they consider that the processing of their data infringes this Regulation.
key_obligations: Any individual can lodge a complaint
The authority must inform of the outcome
Possibility to mandate an organisation
sanctions: No direct sanction - procedural right
practical_examples: Filing a complaint online with the supervisory authority
NOYB regularly files complaints on behalf of EU citizens

chapter: Chapter VIII - Remedies, Liability and Penalties
title: Right to an effective judicial remedy
content: Every data subject has the right to an effective judicial remedy where they consider that their GDPR rights have been infringed.
key_obligations: Right to bring proceedings before the courts
Jurisdiction: place of establishment or data subject's residence
Possibility of collective actions
sanctions: Damages as determined by the court
practical_examples: Legal action by a consumer against a company

chapter: Chapter VIII - Remedies, Liability and Penalties
title: Right to compensation and liability
content: Any person who has suffered material or non-material damage as a result of an infringement of this Regulation has the right to receive compensation.
key_obligations: Joint and several liability of controller and processor
Compensation for material and non-material damage
No cap on damages
sanctions: Damages as determined by the court - no cap
practical_examples: Compensation for disclosure of medical data

chapter: Chapter VIII - Remedies, Liability and Penalties
title: General conditions for imposing administrative fines
content: Administrative fines shall be effective, proportionate and dissuasive. Two tiers: up to EUR 10 million/2% turnover and up to EUR 20 million/4% global annual turnover.
key_obligations: Fines proportionate to the gravity of the violation
Criteria: nature, gravity, duration, intentional character, measures taken
Two tiers of fines
sanctions: Tier 1: EUR 10M/2% turnover. Tier 2: EUR 20M/4% turnover
practical_examples: EUR 1.2 billion fine to Meta in 2023
EUR 746 million fine to Amazon in 2021

chapter: Chapter VIII - Remedies, Liability and Penalties
title: Penalties
content: Member States shall lay down rules on other penalties, including criminal penalties. They shall be effective, proportionate and dissuasive.
key_obligations: Member States may provide for criminal penalties
Notification of penalties to the Commission
sanctions: Criminal penalties according to national law
practical_examples: In France, up to 5 years imprisonment and EUR 300,000 fine under the Criminal Code

title: Processing and freedom of expression
content: Member States shall reconcile data protection with the right to freedom of expression, including for journalism and artistic or literary expression.
key_obligations: Reconcile data protection and freedom of expression
Provide exemptions for journalism
sanctions: No specific sanction
practical_examples: A journalist may process personal data in the course of investigations

title: Processing in the context of employment
content: Member States may provide more specific rules for the processing of employees' personal data in the employment context.
key_obligations: Possibility of more specific national rules for employment
Safeguard human dignity and fundamental rights of employees
sanctions: According to national law
practical_examples: CCTV at work is possible but under strict conditions
Obligation to inform employees and works councils

title: Repeal of Directive 95/46/EC
content: Directive 95/46/EC is repealed with effect from 25 May 2018.
key_obligations: The GDPR replaces Directive 95/46/EC since 25 May 2018
sanctions: No direct sanction
practical_examples: Contracts referencing the Directive must be updated

title: Entry into force and application
content: This Regulation enters into force on 24 May 2016 and applies from 25 May 2018.
key_obligations: Entry into force on 24 May 2016
Mandatory application from 25 May 2018
Directly applicable without transposition
sanctions: No direct sanction
practical_examples: Organisations had two years to achieve compliance

description: Google fined for not allowing users to refuse cookies as easily as they could accept them on google.fr and youtube.com.
article_violated: Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act (ePrivacy Directive)

description: Amazon fined for its non-GDPR-compliant advertising targeting system. The highest fine ever imposed at the time of publication.

violation_type: Unlawful data transfer to the United States
description: Meta fined for transferring Facebook users' personal data to the US without appropriate safeguards. The largest GDPR fine ever imposed.

company: H&M Hennes & Mauritz Online Shop A.B. & Co. KG
description: H&M fined for collecting detailed private information about employees in Nuremberg, including religious beliefs, family issues and health status.
British Airways fined following a 2018 cyberattack compromising data of approximately 400,000 customers. Initial fine of GBP 183 million reduced due to COVID-19.

violation_type: Non-compliance with consent for ad targeting
description: Criteo fined for processing browsing data without valid consent for advertising targeting.
WhatsApp fined for failing to provide users with sufficiently clear and transparent information about data processing.
Instagram fined for non-compliant processing of children's data, including making minors' phone numbers and emails public by default.
Clearview AI fined for collecting facial images of Italian citizens from the internet without legal basis to feed its facial recognition software.

violation_type: Non-compliance with consent and insufficient transparency
description: CaixaBank fined for processing without valid consent and insufficient information, in the context of the merger with Bankia.
IAB Europe fined for its Transparency and Consent Framework deemed non-compliant with the GDPR.

violation_type: Unlawful use of data in employee evaluations
description: RATP fined for using the number of strike days in employee promotion files, constituting processing of trade union activity data.
AG2R fined for excessive data retention and telephone marketing without prior consent.
CNIL fined Clearview AI for collecting photographs of millions of people without consent to feed its facial recognition software.
Marriott fined following the compromise of the Starwood database, exposing data of approximately 339 million customers worldwide.
Carrefour fined for insufficient information, excessive retention periods, obstacles to exercising rights, and non-compliant cookies.
Google fined for placing advertising cookies on google.fr without prior consent.
article_violated: Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act

description: TikTok fined for default privacy settings making children's accounts public and dark patterns in the Family Pairing feature.

company: Uber France SAS and Uber B.V.
description: Uber fined for transferring European drivers' data to the US without appropriate safeguards and multiple compliance failures.

violation_type: Unlawful processing and lack of transparency
description: OpenAI fined for processing personal data in ChatGPT training without proper legal basis, lack of transparency and absence of age verification for minors.
Amazon France fined for excessively intrusive employee surveillance in warehouses using scanners to measure real-time activity and productivity.
Vodafone Spain fined for repeated unsolicited marketing calls including to numbers on the opt-out list.
Microsoft fined for placing advertising cookies on Bing without consent and a defective refusal mechanism.
article_violated: Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act

description: Meta fined following the leak of over 533 million Facebook users' data through scraping due to insufficient privacy settings.
1&1 Telecom fined for insufficient authentication measures in its telephone customer service.

violation_type: Non-compliance with consent and excessive retention
description: Doctissimo fined for collecting health data via quizzes without explicit consent and excessive retention periods.
TikTok fined for not allowing users to refuse cookies as easily as accepting them.
article_violated: Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act

checklist_items: Inform about transfers outside the EU
Conduct DPIA for health data processing
Audit trail for patient record access
Obtain explicit consent for sensitive data
Manage access rights on need-to-know basis
Define CV retention periods (24 months max recommended)
Conduct DPIA if profiling or surveillance
Conduct DPIA for credit scoring and fraud detection
Reconcile GDPR with banking regulations (KYC, AML)
Comply with retention periods (10 years accounting)
Obtain valid consent before email marketing
Respect right to object to marketing
Conduct DPIA for e-services and smart city
Limit supporting documents requested from tenants
Secure financial data of tenants and buyers
Include data processing information in leases
Manage mandates and data sharing between professionals
Respect right to object to marketing
Inform members and donors about data processing
Handle deletion requests from former members
Comply with supervisory authority guidelines for non-profits
Manage customer reviews and associated data
Secure production data containing personal data
Secure data exchanges with industrial partners
Obtain informed consent from study participants
Integrate privacy by design from product conception
Appoint a data protection lead (DPO if mandatory)
Encrypt personal data in transit and at rest
Manage access by least privilege principle
Regulate APIs and third-party data sharing
Prepare GDPR clauses for client and partner contracts
Comply with connection data retention (1 year)
Notify breaches to subscribers and authority
Manage archives according to legal retention
Publish data protection policy on institutional websites
Respect right to be forgotten and delisting
Train journalists on source data protection
Manage photo and video data (image rights)
Mandatory DPIA before AI deployment processing personal data
Provide right to explanation for automated decisions
Implement human intervention for significant decisions
Document potential biases and corrective measures
Regulate use of personal data for model training
Comply with the EU AI Act alongside GDPR
Regularly audit AI models for compliance

context: Deployment of a CCTV system in a shopping centre
risk_description: Disproportionate surveillance of customers and employees, invasion of privacy
mitigation_measures: Limit areas covered (no changing rooms, toilets, break areas)
Access restricted to authorised personnel only

context: Facial recognition system for workplace access control
risk_description: Processing of biometric data (sensitive data Article 9), risk of template leakage, disproportionate employee surveillance
mitigation_measures: Justify necessity compared to less intrusive alternatives (badge, PIN)
Store templates on individual devices (smart card)

context: Launch of a mobile health app collecting medical data
risk_description: Mass collection of sensitive health data, risk of medical data leak, unauthorised access, unintended reuse

context: Customer credit scoring system for loan approval
risk_description: Automated decision significantly affecting individuals (loan refusal), risk of algorithmic discrimination, lack of model transparency
mitigation_measures: Mandatory human intervention before refusal decisions
Annual model performance and fairness review

context: GPS tracking of delivery fleet vehicles
risk_description: Continuous monitoring of driver movements, invasion of privacy, risk of data collection outside working hours
mitigation_measures: Prior information to employees and works council
Access limited to direct management only
Prohibition of use for disciplinary purposes (except proven fraud)

context: Centralised patient database for a hospital group
risk_description: Mass centralisation of health data, risk of large-scale data leak, unauthorised access by non-authorised staff
mitigation_measures: Access compartmentalisation by department and facility
Complete audit trail for all accesses
AES-256 encryption at rest and in transit
Business continuity plan and encrypted backups

context: AI chatbot using customer data for personalised responses
risk_description: Large-scale automated processing, risk of inadvertent data disclosure by chatbot, learning on sensitive data
mitigation_measures: Filter responses to prevent personal data disclosure
Limit conversational context (no long-term memory of sensitive data)
Clear information about automated nature of exchanges
Option to switch to human agent

context: Cross-brand loyalty programme for a retail group
risk_description: Consumer habit profiling, data cross-referencing between brands, targeted marketing without adequate consent
mitigation_measures: Granular consent per brand and processing type
Pseudonymisation of profiles in centralised database
Retention limited to 3 years after last purchase
Full transparency on collected data and use

context: Camera-equipped drones for monitoring a SEVESO industrial site
risk_description: Capturing images of people without consent, disproportionate aerial surveillance, privacy risk for neighbours
mitigation_measures: Limit flights to the site perimeter only
Automatically blur faces and licence plates
Prohibit flights over neighbouring residential areas
Retention limited to 7 days except in case of incident

context: AI-powered fraud detection in an online bank
risk_description: False positives leading to unjustified account blocking, intensive behavioural profiling, automated decisions affecting client rights
mitigation_measures: Mandatory human intervention before account blocking
Transparency about AI use in terms and conditions

context: Generalised remote working with employee monitoring
risk_description: Disproportionate surveillance of employees at home (screenshots, keylogger, permanent webcam), invasion of privacy and home
mitigation_measures: Focus on result-based indicators rather than surveillance
Full employee information and works council consultation
Remote working charter including data protection rules
Strict separation of professional and personal tools

context: Centralised fingerprint database for multi-site access control
risk_description: Centralisation of sensitive biometric data, major risk if compromised, large-scale biometric surveillance
mitigation_measures: Prefer individual storage (smart card) over centralised
AES-256 encryption with master key on HSM
Physical separation of biometric server from main network
Immediate deletion of templates upon employee departure
Double explicit consent with non-biometric alternative

context: Electronic voting system for works council elections
risk_description: Risk of breach of voting secrecy, result manipulation, traceability of individual votes
mitigation_measures: Technical impossibility of linking vote to voter
Sealed retention during legal challenge period

context: AI-powered plagiarism detection tool in a university
risk_description: Processing of personal academic data (student work), storage of copies, false positives leading to unjustified sanctions
mitigation_measures: Mandatory human intervention before any sanction
Retention limited to end of academic year

context: Automated body temperature screening at building entrance
risk_description: Collection of health data (body temperature), risk of discrimination, proportionality concerns
mitigation_measures: No identification of the person during measurement
Alternative provided in case of detection (no automatic access refusal)
Removal of device when health justification ends

context: Dating app collecting data on sexual orientation
risk_description: Sensitive data collection (sexual orientation, Article 9), major risk if leaked, risk to physical safety in certain contexts
mitigation_measures: Explicit and informed consent for sensitive data processing
Profile identity verification to limit fake accounts
Profile hiding option in certain geographic zones
No sharing of sensitive data with third parties

question: What are the six legal bases for processing personal data under the GDPR?
answer: The six legal bases under Article 6 are: 1) Consent; 2) Performance of a contract; 3) Compliance with a legal obligation; 4) Protection of vital interests; 5) Performance of a task in the public interest; 6) Legitimate interests pursued by the controller. Each processing operation must rely on one documented legal basis.

question: How to obtain valid consent under the GDPR?
answer: Consent must be: freely given (no imbalance of power), specific (per purpose), informed (clear information on identity, purposes, data, rights) and unambiguous (positive act, no pre-ticked boxes). The controller must be able to prove consent and the data subject must be able to withdraw at any time as easily as they gave it. For sensitive data, consent must be explicit.

question: What is the deadline for responding to a data subject rights request?
answer: One month from receipt. Extendable by two months for complex requests, provided the data subject is informed within the initial month. If no action is taken, the controller must inform within one month of the reasons and the possibility of lodging a complaint with the authority and seeking judicial remedy.

question: When is DPO appointment mandatory?
answer: Three cases: 1) Public authority or body; 2) Core activities consisting of large-scale regular and systematic monitoring; 3) Core activities consisting of large-scale processing of special categories of data or criminal conviction data. Outside these cases, appointment is recommended but not mandatory.

question: What to do in case of a personal data breach?
answer: 1) Document in the internal breach register; 2) Assess the risk; 3) If risk exists: notify the authority within 72 hours; 4) If high risk: communicate to data subjects without undue delay; 5) Implement corrective measures. Every breach must be documented even without notification.

question: When is a Data Protection Impact Assessment mandatory?
answer: When processing is likely to result in a high risk. Three specified cases: 1) Systematic evaluation with profiling and legal effects; 2) Large-scale processing of sensitive data; 3) Systematic large-scale monitoring of a publicly accessible area. National authorities publish lists of processing types requiring a DPIA.

question: What are the mechanisms for transferring data outside the EU?
answer: By priority: 1) Adequacy decision (Art. 45); 2) Appropriate safeguards (Art. 46): SCCs, BCRs, approved codes of conduct, certifications; 3) Derogations (Art. 49): explicit consent, contract, public interest. Since Schrems II, a Transfer Impact Assessment is required for SCCs and BCRs.

question: What must the records of processing activities contain?
answer: For each processing: name of controller, purposes, categories of data subjects and data, recipients, transfers, retention periods, security measures. Mandatory for organisations with more than 250 employees or in case of non-occasional processing, sensitive data or high-risk processing. In practice, all organisations are recommended to maintain records.

question: What are the obligations of a processor under the GDPR?
answer: The processor must: 1) Process only on documented instructions; 2) Ensure staff confidentiality; 3) Implement security measures; 4) Only engage sub-processors with authorisation; 5) Assist the controller with data subject rights; 6) Assist with security, notification and DPIA; 7) Delete or return data at contract end; 8) Allow audits. All formalised by contract.

question: What are the rules applicable to cookies under the GDPR and ePrivacy?
answer: Clear prior information; consent required for non-essential cookies; refusing must be as easy as accepting; essential cookies are exempt; consent validity typically 6 months; proof of consent must be retained. Non-essential cookies include advertising, analytics and social media cookies.

question: How to determine data retention periods?
answer: Based on: 1) Legal obligations (e.g., 10 years accounting, 5 years contracts); 2) Sector-specific guidance from authorities; 3) Operational necessity (time strictly necessary for the purpose). Data can then be archived for legal obligations or litigation, then permanently archived (anonymised) or deleted. The data lifecycle must be documented.

question: What are the categories of sensitive data and their processing conditions?
answer: Article 9: racial/ethnic origin, political opinions, religious/philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, genetic data, biometric data, health data, sex life/sexual orientation. Processing prohibited except: explicit consent, employment law, vital interests, data made public, legal claims, substantial public interest, health/social care, archiving/research/statistics.

question: What technical security measures should be implemented?
answer: 1) Encryption (AES-256, TLS 1.2+); 2) Pseudonymisation/anonymisation; 3) Strict access control (MFA, least privilege); 4) Logging; 5) 3-2-1 backups; 6) Firewalls, antivirus, IDS/IPS; 7) Patch management; 8) Network segmentation; 9) Penetration testing; 10) BCP/DRP. Measures adapted to the risk level.

question: How to implement privacy by design in an IT project?
answer: At each stage: Design (identify necessary data, legal basis, security measures); Development (pseudonymise test data, code review); Testing (consent mechanisms, rights exercise, SAST/DAST); Deployment (maximum privacy settings by default); Operation (monitoring, incidents, audits). Document design choices.

question: How to respond to a data portability request?
answer: Applies to data provided by the data subject, processed automatically, based on consent or contract. Steps: 1) Verify identity; 2) Identify data concerned; 3) Provide in structured format (CSV, JSON, XML); 4) If requested, transmit directly to another controller; 5) Respond within one month; 6) Free of charge. Does not apply to derived data.

question: What evidence of compliance is needed for accountability?
answer: 1) Processing records; 2) DPIAs; 3) Internal policies; 4) Processor contracts (Art. 28); 5) Consent records; 6) Rights management procedures; 7) Breach register; 8) Training records; 9) Audits and action plans; 10) Technical security documentation; 11) Certifications; 12) DPO appointment records.

question: What are the rules governing profiling?
answer: Three levels: 1) Simple profiling (no decision): general GDPR rules; 2) Profiling with human-assisted decision: inform of underlying logic; 3) Solely automated decision with significant effects (Art. 22): prohibited except explicit consent, contractual necessity or legal authorisation. In all cases: right to object, transparency, human intervention possible.

question: What are the two tiers of GDPR fines?
answer: Tier 1 (Art. 83(4)): EUR 10M or 2% turnover for violations of controller/processor obligations (Art. 8, 11, 25-39, 42, 43). Tier 2 (Art. 83(5)): EUR 20M or 4% turnover for violations of principles (Art. 5-7, 9), data subject rights (Art. 12-22), transfers (Art. 44-49). Criteria: nature, gravity, duration, intent, measures taken, history, cooperation.

question: When can legitimate interest be used as a legal basis?
answer: Legitimate interest (Art. 6(1)(f)) requires a three-step balancing test: 1) Identify the legitimate interest (fraud prevention, network security, direct marketing to existing customers); 2) Verify necessity of processing; 3) Balance against data subject rights and interests. Cannot be used by public authorities for their tasks. Right to object always applies.

question: How to audit a processor for GDPR compliance?
answer: Cover: 1) Documentary (security policy, certifications ISO 27001/SOC 2, records, BCP); 2) Technical (encryption, access control, logging, pentests); 3) Organisational (training, DPO, rights and breach procedures); 4) Contractual (Art. 28 clauses, sub-processors); 5) Transfers (data location, mechanisms for non-EU). Internal or external audit.

question: Is the DPO personally liable for non-compliance?
answer: No. The controller bears responsibility for compliance (Art. 24). The DPO informs, advises and monitors. The DPO is protected: cannot be dismissed or penalised for performing their tasks (Art. 38(3)). Confirmed by the CJEU (Leistritz C-534/20). However, the DPO must perform duties with diligence.

question: Can a data erasure request be refused?
answer: Yes. The right to erasure is not absolute. Refusal is possible for: 1) Freedom of expression; 2) Legal obligation to retain; 3) Public health interest; 4) Archiving, research, statistics; 5) Legal claims. The controller must inform within one month of the reasons and available remedies (complaint to authority, judicial remedy).

question: What is the Schrems II ruling and its practical consequences?
answer: CJEU ruling of 16 July 2020 (C-311/18) invalidating the EU-US Privacy Shield. US legislation (FISA 702, EO 12333) found insufficient. SCCs remain valid but require a Transfer Impact Assessment per case. Since July 2023, the EU-US Data Privacy Framework replaces the Privacy Shield for certified US companies.

question: How to establish and maintain a breach register?
answer: For each breach: date of discovery, nature (confidentiality/integrity/availability), description and circumstances, categories and number of persons affected, probable consequences, corrective measures, notification decision (with justification if not notified), communication decision to data subjects, follow-up actions. Digital format, available to authority on request.

question: Which cookies are exempt from consent?
answer: Strictly necessary cookies: 1) Authentication (session); 2) Shopping basket; 3) Interface personalisation (language); 4) Security; 5) Load balancing; 6) Media player (session); 7) Certain anonymous audience measurement under strict conditions. All others (advertising, social media, non-anonymous analytics) require prior consent.

question: What types of processing generally require a DPIA?
answer: Processing involving: 1) Health data at scale; 2) Genetic data; 3) Profiling with adverse effects; 4) Biometric data; 5) Systematic employee surveillance; 6) Large-scale location data; 7) Data of vulnerable persons; 8) Large-scale data cross-referencing; 9) AI with legal effects; 10) Exclusion from rights or contracts; 11) Social alert systems; 12) Scoring/evaluation; 13) Pooled contractual breach records; 14) Sensitive zone access control.
regulatory_reference: Article 35(4) GDPR and national authority lists

question: Pseudonymisation vs anonymisation: what are the differences?
answer: Pseudonymisation: data not attributable without additional information (correspondence key). Remains personal data under GDPR. Anonymisation: identification impossible irreversibly. Falls outside GDPR scope. Anonymisation criteria: resistance to singling out, linkability and inference. Pseudonymisation is an encouraged security measure (Art. 25, 32).

question: How to achieve GDPR compliance from scratch?
answer: Steps: 1) Map all processing; 2) Assess gaps; 3) Prioritise actions; 4) Appoint DPO if mandatory; 5) Conduct DPIAs; 6) Update processor contracts; 7) Draft information notices and policies; 8) Implement rights and breach management processes; 9) Secure processing; 10) Train staff; 11) Document compliance (accountability); 12) Ongoing monitoring and audits.

question: How to verify identity for a data subject rights request?
answer: Verification must be proportionate: if already identified (logged in), no additional ID needed. If reasonable doubt: request ID document. Do not systematically request ID if other means suffice. Delete the ID document after verification. If identity cannot be confirmed, explain the refusal and indicate available remedies.

question: Are SMEs with fewer than 250 employees exempt from the GDPR?
answer: No. The GDPR applies to all organisations processing personal data. Article 30(5) provides a limited records exception (under 250 employees), but it practically never applies since any HR or customer processing is non-occasional. All organisations are recommended to maintain records, and simplified templates are available.

question: How does the GDPR apply to artificial intelligence systems?
answer: Fully applicable: 1) Legal basis for collection and use; 2) Training data minimisation; 3) Transparency about AI use; 4) Article 22: human intervention and right to explanation for automated decisions; 5) Mandatory DPIA for high-risk AI; 6) Privacy by design; 7) Right to object. The EU AI Act (2024) adds specific requirements by risk level.
regulatory_reference: Articles 5, 6, 22, 25, 35 GDPR and EU AI Act 2024

question: How to manage consent withdrawal?
answer: Withdrawal must be as easy as giving consent. Steps: 1) Easily accessible mechanism; 2) Withdrawal does not affect prior lawfulness; 3) Immediately cease processing; 4) Delete data if sole legal basis; 5) Inform processors and recipients; 6) Document; 7) Do not penalise the person. If another legal basis exists, processing may continue.

question: Can the DPO hold other roles simultaneously?
answer: Yes, but without conflicts of interest (Art. 38(6)). Incompatible roles: CEO, CFO, marketing director, HR director, CIO, or any role determining processing purposes and means. The DPO cannot be in a position of self-review. In SMEs, combination with legal or compliance roles (not directorial) is possible, provided independence is guaranteed.
